Find the area ${A}_{\text{max}}$ of the largest rectangle that can be inscribed in the closed region bounded by the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis, and the graph of $y=18-{x}^{2},$ as shown above. Do not round the answer.

${A}_{\text{max}}=$
{{field-1}}
question.worked_solution:
Let $x$ and $y$ be the width and height of the rectangle, respectively. Given a width $x,$ the height $y$ of the rectangle rises up to the curve $y=18-{x}^{2}.$

We want to maximize the area of the rectangle, which is given by

$$
A=xy=x(18-{x}^{2})=18x-{x}^{3}.
$$

Let's compute the critical points. Taking the derivative of the area, we get

$$
{A}^{′}(x)=18-3{x}^{2},
$$

and solving ${A}^{′}(x)=0$ gives the following critical point:

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}^{′}(x) & =0 \\ 18-3{x}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2} & =6 \\ x & =\sqrt{6}\end{aligned}
$$

All that's left now is to confirm that $x=\sqrt{6}$ does indeed give a maximum value of $A(x).$ To do this, we use the first derivative test. We write up a table of values:

| Interval | $(0,\sqrt{6})$ | $\sqrt{6}$ | $(\sqrt{6},3\sqrt{2})$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $1$ | $$ | $4$ |
| ${A}^{′}$ | $+$ | $0$ | $-$ |
| $A$ | $↗$ | $\text{max}$ | $↘$ |

So, $x=\sqrt{6}$ does indeed give a maximum, and the area of the resulting rectangle will be the largest possible.

Therefore, the greatest area ${A}_{\text{max}}$ that a rectangle can have is

$$
\begin{aligned}{A}_{\text{max}}=A(\sqrt{6}) & =18(\sqrt{6})-{(\sqrt{6})}^{3} \\  & =18\sqrt{6}-6\sqrt{6} \\  & =12\sqrt{6}.\end{aligned}
$$
